## What is GitHub

- A website for hosting files and tracking versions over time
- Example: [FIT Retail Index](https://github.com/calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks)
- Built on Git - version tracking for your files
- Lets you publish web apps for free, with no traditional server
- Used for collaboration, portfolios, and class projects
- [github.com](https://github.com/)

## Repositories and Collaborators

- A Repository is a project folder stored on GitHub, with full history
- Each repository has an owner - a user or organization account
- Collaborators are other GitHub users invited to work on the repository
- Collaborators can edit code, fix bugs, and add features together
- Example: [FIT Retail Index](https://github.com/calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks)

## Public Repositories and Private Repositories

- Public Repositories - anyone on the internet can see the code
  - Good for open source, portfolios, and free web hosting
  - Example: class demos and published apps
- Private Repositories - only you and your collaborators can see it
  - Good for homework, drafts, and work in progress
  - You control who is invited as a collaborator

## Create a Repository from Scratch

1. Sign in to GitHub and click **New repository**
2. Give the repository a short, descriptive name
3. Choose **Public** or **Private**
4. Select **Add a README file**
5. Click **Create repository**

The new repository starts with a `README.md` file on the `main` branch.

## Add a Collaborator

1. Open the repository and select **Settings**
2. Select **Collaborators** under **Access**
3. Click **Add people** and enter their GitHub username
4. Send the invitation
5. Ask the collaborator to accept the invitation
6. Return to **Collaborators** and confirm that the invitation was accepted

An invitation does not grant access until the collaborator accepts it.

## Edit an Existing File

1. Open `README.md`
2. Click the pencil icon to edit the file
3. Add a description of the project
4. Click **Commit changes**
5. Enter a short commit message
6. Select **Commit directly to the `main` branch**

## Create a New File

1. Select **Add file** > **Create new file**
2. Enter a filename, such as `notes.md`
3. Add some content to the file
4. Click **Commit changes**
5. Describe the change and commit it directly to `main`

## Delete a File

1. Open the file you want to remove
2. Open the file menu and select **Delete file**
3. Click **Commit changes**
4. Describe why the file is being removed
5. Commit the deletion directly to `main`

Git remembers the deleted file in the repository's history.

## Check Your Work on `main`

- Confirm that the correct files appear in the repository
- Open `README.md` and check the latest edits
- Select **Commits** to see the history
- Open a commit to see which lines were added, changed, or deleted
- Notice that every file operation becomes part of the project history

## Open Source Example: BusMgmtBenchmarks

- [calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks](https://github.com/calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks) - a public, open source repo
- MIT License - anyone can use, copy, and build on the code
- README describes the project, data, and live web app
- 247 commits show the full history of changes over time
- Live site published for free: [FIT Retail Index](https://calvinw.github.io/BusMgmtBenchmarks/)

## Version Control

- Version control tracks every change to your files over time
- Each saved checkpoint is called a commit, with a message describing it
- You can see history, compare versions, and undo mistakes
- Multiple people can work on the same files without losing work

## Branches on GitHub

- A branch is a separate copy of your code for working on something new
- The main branch is the official, working version of the project
- Create a branch to fix a bug or try a feature without breaking main
- When done, merge the branch back into main

## Create and Work on a Branch

1. Open the branch menu, which currently says `main`
2. Type a new branch name, such as `add-about-file`
3. Select **Create branch**
4. Confirm that the branch menu shows the new branch
5. Create a file named `about.md`
6. Commit the new file to the branch

The file is now on the new branch, but not yet on `main`.

## Merge the Branch into `main`

1. Open a **Pull Request** from the new branch into `main`
2. Review the **Files changed** tab
3. Click **Merge pull request**
4. Confirm the merge
5. Return to `main` and confirm that `about.md` is there
6. Delete the merged branch

The commits remain in the history even after the branch is deleted.

## GitHub Pages

- GitHub Pages publishes your repository as a free website
- No traditional server needed - just HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files
- Repo: [calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks](https://github.com/calvinw/BusMgmtBenchmarks)
- Live Pages site: [FIT Retail Index](https://calvinw.github.io/BusMgmtBenchmarks/)
- Address is username.github.io/repository-name

## Creating a Repo from a Template

- Starts your own new repo as a copy of a template repo
- Copies the files, folders, and setup - without the old history
- Lets every student start from the same working project
- Your copy is yours - make it private, add collaborators, and edit freely
